claim: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates the selective transport of large biomolecules through the nuclear envelope.
source: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates the selective transport of large biomolecules through the nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology stated in the abstract.

claim: NPC mimics were constructed by functionalizing the pore walls of freestanding palladium zero-mode waveguides with the FG-nucleoporin Nsp1.
source: As a model system for nuclear transport, we construct NPC mimics by functionalizing the pore walls of freestanding palladium zero-mode waveguides with the FG-nucleoporin Nsp1.
evidence: The experimental approach is described in the abstract and detailed in the methods section.

claim: The approach enables the measurement of single-molecule translocations through individual pores using optical detection.
source: This approach enables the measurement of single-molecule translocations through individual pores using optical detection.
evidence: The capability of the method is demonstrated through the experimental results presented.

claim: Pores below 55 ± 5 nm show significant selectivity that gradually decreases for larger pores.
source: Pores below 55 ± 5 nm show significant selectivity that gradually decreases for larger pores.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: Leakage of BSA occurs by diffusion through transient openings within the dynamic mesh.
source: This finding is corroborated by coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of the Nsp1 mesh within the pore, which suggest that leakage of BSA occurs by diffusion through transient openings within the dynamic mesh.
evidence: This is supported by CGMD simulations and void analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: BSA permeation is modulated when varying the concentration of Kap95.
source: Furthermore, we experimentally observe a modulation of the BSA permeation when varying the concentration of Kap95.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: The central channel of the NPC is lined with intrinsically disordered proteins that are rich in phenylalanine–glycine (FG) repeats, termed FG-Nups.
source: The central channel of this large protein complex (52 MDa in yeast to about 120 MDa in humans, Reichelt et al., 1990; Kim et al., 2018) is lined with intrinsically disordered proteins that are rich in phenylalanine–glycine (FG) repeats, termed FG-Nups.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: The NPC mass is 52 MDa in yeast and about 120 MDa in humans.
source: The central channel of this large protein complex (52 MDa in yeast to about 120 MDa in humans, Reichelt et al., 1990; Kim et al., 2018)
evidence: This is cited from Reichelt et al., 1990 and Kim et al., 2018.

claim: The FG-Nups form a selective barrier that facilitates the transport of dedicated nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) while blocking other proteins.
source: The central transporter mesh constituted by these FG-Nups forms a selective barrier that facilitates the transport of dedicated nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) while blocking other proteins (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Kim et al., 2018.

claim: The inner diameter of the central transporter can dilate from 40 nm to 70 nm under different stress conditions.
source: Recently, it has been discovered that the inner diameter of the central transporter is variable and can dilate from 40 nm to 70 nm under different stress conditions (Zimmerli et al., 2021; Akey et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from Zimmerli et al., 2021 and Akey et al., 2022.

claim: The NPC enables transport rates of approximately 1000 molecules per second.
source: Remarkably, the NPC poses this selective barrier while enabling very high transport rates of ∼1000 molecules per second that traverse the pore, referred to as the 'transport paradox' (Beck and Hurt, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Beck and Hurt, 2017.

claim: Translocation of biomolecules is increasingly hindered above a diameter of approximately 5 nm or a mass of 30-40 kDa.
source: Whereas small molecules pass through the NPC channel without much obstruction, translocation of larger biomolecules is increasingly hindered in a continuous manner above a diameter of ∼5 nm or a mass of ∼30 kDa to 40 kDa, which leads to an effective blockade for large molecules unless they specifically interact with the FG-Nups mesh (Keminer and Peters, 1999; Mohr et al., 2009; Schmidt and Görlich, 2016; Popken et al., 2015; Timney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources: Keminer and Peters, 1999; Mohr et al., 2009; Schmidt and Görlich, 2016; Popken et al., 2015; Timney et al., 2016.

claim: NTRs engage in multivalent interactions with the FG-repeats in the central transporter.
source: The efficient transport of large cargoes that carry a nuclear localization signal is facilitated by NTRs, which engage in multivalent interactions with the FG-repeats in the central transporter (Aramburu and Lemke, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Aramburu and Lemke, 2017.

claim: The Kap95–Kap60 system in yeast (Impβ–Impα in humans) is responsible for the import of proteins into the nucleus.
source: One of the most studied systems is the Kap95–Kap60 system in yeast (Impβ–Impα in humans), responsible for the import of proteins into the nucleus (Görlich and Kutay, 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Görlich and Kutay, 1999.

claim: A selective barrier with similar properties as the native NPC can be reconstituted using even a single native FG-Nup.
source: Using minimal biomimetic systems, it has been shown that a selective barrier with similar properties as the native NPC can be reconstituted using even a single native FG-Nup (Frey and Görlich, 2007; Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009; Kowalczyk et al., 2011; Ananth et al., 2018; Celetti et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2023b) or artificial mimics thereof (Fragasso et al., 2021; Ng et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: Probing translocations through the FG-Nup mesh using solid-state nanopores grafted with FG-Nups was pioneered by Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009 using optical detection of fluorescently tagged molecules.
source: Probing translocations through the FG-Nup mesh using solid-state nanopores grafted with FG-Nups was pioneered by Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009 using optical detection of fluorescently tagged molecules.
evidence: This is cited from Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009.

claim: The previous optical approach by Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009 was limited to bulk measurements of transport through porous membranes that contained many pores in parallel, lacking single-pore and single-molecule resolution.
source: However, this approach was limited to bulk measurements of transport through porous membranes that contained many such pores in parallel, thus lacking single-pore and single-molecule resolution.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work cited from Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009.

claim: Conductance-based nanopore measurements offer single-molecule sensitivity but remain restricted to pore sizes around 30–50 nm.
source: While this approach offers single-molecule sensitivity, the current-based readout remains unspecific (i.e., cannot distinguish different proteins), requires the application of a bias voltage, which may influence the transport rate and speed of the translocations, and offers limited signal-to-noise ratio. It remains therefore restricted to pore sizes around 30–50 nm where the translocation of single molecules leads to a detectable current drop.
evidence: This is a comparison with conductance-based methods cited from Kowalczyk et al., 2011; Ananth et al., 2018; Fragasso et al., 2021.

claim: The fluorescence-based assay is based on freestanding palladium nanopores that act as zero-mode waveguides.
source: Here, we implement a fluorescence-based assay for the simultaneous detection of single-molecule translocations of different molecular species through solid-state metal nanopores made of palladium, based on our previous work (Klughammer and Dekker, 2021).
evidence: This is the method described in the manuscript, building on previous work.

claim: The nanopores block the propagation of 485 nm and 640 nm wavelength excitation light through the metal membrane.
source: The < 200 nm nanopores act as zero-mode waveguides (ZMW, Levene et al., 2003) that block the propagation of the 485 nm and 640 nm wavelength excitation light through the metal membrane.
evidence: This is a property of the ZMW pores demonstrated in the FDTD simulations in Figure 2.

claim: The method does not require a bias voltage as it relies solely on the free diffusion of the fluorescent molecules.
source: Notably, our method does not require a bias voltage as it relies solely on the free diffusion of the fluorescent molecules, nor does the detection efficiency depend on the pore diameter.
evidence: This is a feature of the experimental approach described.

claim: The detection efficiency does not depend on the pore diameter.
source: Notably, our method does not require a bias voltage as it relies solely on the free diffusion of the fluorescent molecules, nor does the detection efficiency depend on the pore diameter.
evidence: This is a feature of the experimental approach demonstrated in the FDTD simulations.

claim: The selectivity of Nsp1-coated pores decreases with pore diameter, with the main loss of selectivity happening at about a diameter of 55 nm.
source: We find that the selectivity of Nsp1-coated pores decreases with pore diameter, with the main loss of selectivity happening at about a diameter of 55 nm.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For smaller pores, selectivity arises because Kap95 proteins can efficiently cross the FG-Nup mesh while BSA transport is hindered.
source: Selectivity for smaller pores arises because Kap95 proteins can efficiently cross the FG-Nup mesh in the pore while BSA transport is hindered.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: For larger pores, transport selectivity is gradually lost due to increasing leakage of BSA.
source: For larger pores, transport selectivity is gradually lost due to increasing leakage of BSA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: CGMD simulations show that the loss of selectivity is due to the formation of voids within the Nsp1 mesh of comparable size to BSA molecules.
source: Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations reproduce these experimental findings and show that the loss of selectivity is due to the formation of voids within the Nsp1 mesh if comparable size to BSA molecules.
evidence: This is a finding from the CGMD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: For small pores, voids in the Nsp1 mesh are transient, whereas for large pores they become persistent and a central channel forms.
source: For small pores, these voids are transient, whereas for large pores they become persistent and a central channel forms.
evidence: This is a finding from the CGMD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Upon increasing the concentration of Kap95, a moderate increase of the transport selectivity is observed for pores with a diameter below 50 nm.
source: Upon increasing the concentration of the transporter Kap95 in the experiment, we observe a moderate increase of the transport selectivity for pores with a diameter below 50 nm.
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6.

claim: The event rate of BSA translocations for large pores increases with Kap95 concentration.
source: Intriguingly, we find that the event rate of BSA translocations for large pores increases with Kap95 concentration, suggesting that filling the FG-Nup mesh with NTRs reduces the selective volume.
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6.

claim: Filling the FG-Nup mesh with NTRs reduces the selective volume.
source: Intriguingly, we find that the event rate of BSA translocations for large pores increases with Kap95 concentration, suggesting that filling the FG-Nup mesh with NTRs reduces the selective volume.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Fabrication of the metal membranes was achieved by evaporating a layer of Pd onto a SiNx membrane that was subsequently removed by reactive ion etching.
source: Fabrication of the metal membranes was achieved by evaporating a layer of Pd onto a SiNx membrane (20 nm thickness) that was subsequently removed by reactive ion etching (in a process that was slightly adapted from Klughammer and Dekker, 2021, see section 'Fabrication of freestanding Pd ZMWs' for details).
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: After processing, the Pd membrane had a thickness of approximately 90 nm.
source: After processing, the Pd membrane had a thickness of ≈ 90 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: A cleaning step was required to remove impurities from the Pd surface prior to thiol binding to ensure efficient surface grafting.
source: After the FIB-milling step, a cleaning step was required to remove impurities from the Pd surface prior to thiol binding to ensure efficient surface grafting.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: A gentle cleaning protocol was developed that used either hydrogen peroxide or boiling ethanol.
source: Since previous protocols relied on freshly prepared surfaces, we developed a gentle cleaning protocol that used either hydrogen peroxide or boiling ethanol, inspired by Majid et al., 2003 (see 'Materials and methods' and Appendix 1).
evidence: This is described in the methods section and cited from Majid et al., 2003.

claim: The cleaning step ensured that the Pd surface was competent for thiol binding, as validated by QCM-D experiments and surface plasmon resonance measurements.
source: The cleaning step ensured that the Pd surface was competent for thiol binding, as validated by quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring (QCM-D) experiments (see Appendix 1—figures 1–3) and surface plasmon resonance measurements (Andersson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is validated by QCM-D experiments and cited from Andersson et al., 2022.

claim: The cleaning procedure does not alter the pore shape or close the pores, as confirmed by transmission electron microscopy.
source: We additionally confirmed that the cleaning procedure does not alter the pore shape or closes the pores by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (cf. images shown in Klughammer et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is confirmed by TEM imaging cited from Klughammer et al., 2023b.

claim: Open pores were passivated using (1-mercaptoundec-11-yl)hexa(ethylene glycol) (MUHEG) to prevent unspecific sticking of proteins to the metal surface.
source: To prevent unspecific sticking of proteins to the metal surface, the control open pores were passivated using (1-mercaptoundec-11-yl)hexa(ethylene glycol) (MUHEG), which forms a self-assembled monolayer by thiol-Pd binding enhanced with a dense packing due to the hydrophobic interactions between the alkane groups while providing a hydrophilic surface through the terminal hexaethylene glycol groups (Prime and Whitesides, 1993, Figure 1A, top).
evidence: This is described in the methods section and cited from Prime and Whitesides, 1993.

claim: Coating of the biomimetic pores was performed with Nsp1 containing a C-terminal cysteine at a concentration of 1 µM.
source: Coating of the biomimetic pores was performed with Nsp1 containing a C-terminal cysteine at a concentration of 1 µM.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: The lower limit for the grafting distance in the pore is expected to be 6.5 nm as measured previously by surface plasmon resonance experiments on flat gold surfaces.
source: We expect a lower limit for the grafting distance in the pore of 6.5 nm as measured previously by surface plasmon resonance experiments on flat gold surfaces (Fragasso et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from Fragasso et al., 2022.

claim: Additional passivation of the remaining free area between Nsp1 molecules was achieved using short thiolated 350 Da PEG molecules.
source: Additional passivation of the remaining free area between Nsp1 molecules was achieved using short thiolated 350 Da PEG molecules (Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009; Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2014, Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: This is described in the methods section and cited from Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009; Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2014.

claim: A constant flow was applied to the lower detection side to avoid accumulation of fluorescently labeled molecules.
source: After functionalization, the palladium membrane was mounted in a flow cell made of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), which provides a reservoir on the upper side for the addition of analyte, as well as a flow channel on the lower detection side to which a constant flow was applied to avoid accumulation of fluorescently labeled molecules (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: A change point detection algorithm was adapted for accurate and unbiased detection of the signal spikes originating from single-molecule translocation.
source: For accurate and unbiased detection of the signal spikes originating from single-molecule translocation, we adapted a change point detection algorithm (Watkins and Yang, 2005) that takes full advantage of the single-photon information, as described previously in Klughammer and Dekker, 2021.
evidence: This is described in the methods section and cited from Watkins and Yang, 2005 and Klughammer and Dekker, 2021.

claim: The applied pressure induces a hydrodynamic flow that acts against the concentration gradient and results in an approximate reduction of the measured event rates by 5%.
source: Note that the applied pressure induces a hydrodynamic flow that acts against the concentration gradient and results in an approximate reduction of the measured event rates by 5% (Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Appendix 3—figure 2.

claim: A total of eight pores were milled into the Pd membrane, each surrounded by partially milled markers that facilitate the localization of the nanopores in a bright-field image.
source: To improve the throughput of the measurements, a linear array of eight pores of varying size was milled into the palladium membrane, and these pores were probed consecutively during the experiments.
evidence: This is described in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Crosstalk between pores was minimized by applying a flow orthogonal to the pore array, resulting in a false detection rate of less than 2%.
source: Crosstalk between pores was minimized by applying a flow orthogonal to the pore array, resulting in a false detection rate of less than 2 % (Appendix 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Appendix 3.

claim: Fluorescence time traces show efficient translocations for both Kap95 and BSA through the open pore.
source: The recorded time traces of Kap95 labeled with the Alexa Fluor 647 dye (Alexa647, orange) at a concentration of 100 nM and BSA labeled with the Alexa Fluor 488 dye (Alexa488, blue) at a concentration of 250 nM show efficient translocations for both proteins through the open pore (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Kap95 still translocated through the Nsp1-coated pore at a high rate, while BSA was clearly hindered.
source: While Kap95 still translocated through the Nsp1-coated pore at a high rate, BSA was clearly hindered as is evident from the reduction of the number of signal spikes in the time trace (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: For each pore, a total of three different concentrations of BSA (0 nM, 250 nM, and 500 nM) and Kap95 (0 nM, 100 nM, and 1000 nM) were probed, resulting in nine different conditions tested consecutively.
source: For each pore, we probed a total of three different concentrations of BSA (0 nM, 250 nM, and 500 nM) and Kap95 (0 nM, 100 nM, and 1000 nM ), and all combinations thereof. This resulted in nine different conditions that were tested consecutively (see Figure 3E and F, bottom)
evidence: This is described in the results section and shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: For the open pore, the selectivity is 0.73±0.05.
source: For the open pore, we find a selectivity of 0.73±0.05.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: A selectivity value between 0.7 and 0.8 is expected for open pores due to the smaller size and thus faster diffusivity of BSA, leading to a higher translocation rate compared to Kap95.
source: A selectivity value between 0.7 and 0.8 is expected due to the smaller size and thus faster diffusivity of BSA, leading to a higher translocation rate compared to Kap95 (see Appendix 5—figure 1E).
evidence: This is explained in the results section and shown in Appendix 5—figure 1E.

claim: The Nsp1-coated pore shows a selectivity of 6.3±1.0, indicating a clear selectivity induced by the Nsp1 coating.
source: By contrast, the Nsp1-coated pore shows a significantly higher value of 6.3±1.0), indicating a clear selectivity induced by the Nsp1 coating.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: A total of 46 pores with diameters ranging from 35 nm to 160 nm were measured, which were either open or coated with Nsp1.
source: We measured the normalized event rates and apparent selectivity of a total of 46 pores with diameters ranging from 35 nm to 160 nm, which were either open or coated with Nsp1 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: For pores above 80 nm diameter, it was necessary to reduce the fraction of labeled proteins fivefold to avoid too high event rates that would lead to nonlinearity in the event detection due to overlapping events.
source: Note that for pores above 80 nm diameter, it was necessary to reduce the fraction of labeled proteins fivefold in order to avoid too high event rates that would lead to nonlinearity in the event detection due to overlapping events.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The normalized event rate for Kap95 did not change significantly between open and Nsp1-coated pores.
source: For Kap95, the translocation rate through Nsp1-coated pores was reduced by only about 10% compared to open pores (see Figure 4 and Appendix 6—figure 2E). In other words, we observed no significant reduction of the normalized event rate for Nsp1-coated pores compared to open pores (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and C and Appendix 6—figure 2E.

claim: No reduced diffusivity of Kap95 molecules on the pore exit side was observed, as quantified by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS).
source: Interestingly, we also observed no reduced diffusivity of Kap95 molecules on the pore exit side, as quantified by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) (Appendix 7—figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Appendix 7—figure 1A and B.

claim: A shortening of the fluorescence lifetime of Kap95–Alexa647 for Nsp1-coated pores compared to open pores was observed, which was not observed for BSA–Alexa488.
source: However, we observed a shortening of the fluorescence lifetime of Kap95–Alexa647 for Nsp1-coated pores compared to open pores, which was not observed for BSA–Alexa488 (Appendix 7—figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Appendix 7—figure 1C and D.

claim: The shortening of the fluorescence lifetime indicates that, on the exit side, Kap95 diffuses closer to the pore walls compared to BSA due to interactions with the Nsp1 mesh.
source: As the fluorescence lifetime is shortened in the proximity of the metal nanostructure (see Appendix 2—figure 4), this indicates that, on the exit side, Kap95 diffuses closer to the pore walls compared to BSA due to interactions with the Nsp1 mesh.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence lifetime data.

claim: For BSA, the normalized event rates for Nsp1-coated pores were significantly reduced, especially at small-pore diameters.
source: For BSA, the normalized event rates for Nsp1-coated pores were, by contrast, significantly reduced, especially at small-pore diameters (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: An approximately tenfold reduction of the event rate was observed for Nsp1-coated pores with a diameter of 35 nm, whereas only a twofold reduction was observed for pores with a diameter of 100 nm.
source: More specifically, we observed an approximately tenfold reduction of the event rate for Nsp1-coated pores with a diameter of 35 nm, whereas only a twofold reduction was observed for pores with a diameter of 100 nm, which further decreases for larger pores (Appendix 6—figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Appendix 6—figure 2E.

claim: Normalized event rates for open pores were well described by the quadratic function Equation 2.
source: Normalized event rates for open pores were well described by the quadratic function Equation 2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The BSA data for Nsp1-coated pores could not be described using the quadratic dependence with a single scaling factor over the whole range of pore diameters due to the steep increase of the event rate for larger pores.
source: However, the BSA data for Nsp1-coated pores could not be described using the quadratic dependence with a single scaling factor over the whole range of pore diameters due to the steep increase of the event rate for larger pores (Appendix 6—figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Appendix 6—figure 2B and D.

claim: For open pores, the selectivity ratio is 0.70±0.02, independent of the pore diameter.
source: For open pores, we find a selectivity ratio of 0.70±0.02, independent of the pore diameter.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: For Nsp1-coated pores below 50 nm, selectivity ratios of individual pores ranged between 2.1±0.4 and 6.3±1.0, which is 3–9 times higher than for open pores.
source: For Nsp1-coated pores below 50 nm, selectivity ratios of individual pores ranged between 2.1±0.4 and 6.3±1.0, which is 3–9 times higher than for open pores.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: For pores larger than 60 nm, a gradual decrease of the selectivity ratio with increasing pore diameter is observed from 1.7±0.2 to a value of 0.7±0.2 for the largest pores.
source: For pores larger than 60 nm, we see a gradual decrease of the selectivity ratio with increasing pore diameter from 1.7±0.2 to a value of 0.7±0.2 for the largest pores, which approaches the selectivity ratio of open pores.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The finite selectivity for large pores suggests that the Nsp1 coating on the pore walls still hindered the translocation of BSA, even after most of the selectivity was lost.
source: The finite selectivity for large pores suggests that the Nsp1 coating on the pore walls still hindered the translocation of BSA, even after most of the selectivity was lost.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 4E.

claim: CGMD simulations were performed with the implicit-solvent 1BPA-1.1 model for intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: CGMD simulations were performed with the implicit-solvent 1BPA-1.1 model for intrinsically disordered proteins (Ghavami et al., 2013; Ghavami et al., 2014; Jafarinia et al., 2020; Jafarinia et al., 2022; Dekker et al., 2023).
evidence: This is described in the methods section and cited from multiple sources.

claim: A void analysis method was applied to predict translocation rates based on the equilibrium fluctuations of the Nsp1 mesh in the absence of Kap95 or BSA.
source: To obtain statistically meaningful estimates of the translocation rates, we applied a void analysis method developed by Winogradoff et al., 2022. Rather than explicitly simulating translocation events of BSA molecules through the Nsp1 mesh, we used this theoretical approach to predict translocation rates based on the equilibrium fluctuations of the Nsp1 mesh in the absence of Kap95 or BSA.
evidence: This is described in the methods section and cited from Winogradoff et al., 2022.

claim: Simulations were performed of nanopores with a length of 90 nm and diameters in the range of 40–160 nm.
source: We performed simulations of nanopores with a length of 90 nm and diameters in the range of 40–160 nm.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: Nsp1 proteins were anchored at their C-terminus to the interior wall of the nanopore scaffold in a close-packed triangular distribution.
source: Nsp1 proteins were then grafted to the scaffold wall at their C-terminal Cys-residue, with the N-terminus of the Nsp1 proteins pointing out of the nanopore occlusion.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: The best match between the experimental and calculated BSA event rates over the whole range of probed diameters was obtained at a grafting density of 1 Nsp1 per 300 nm².
source: The best match between the experimental and calculated BSA event rates over the whole range of probed diameters was obtained at a grafting density of 1 Nsp1 per 300 nm2 (Figure 5D and Appendix 10—figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5D and Appendix 10—figure 3A and B.

claim: The estimated grafting density is approximately one order of magnitude lower compared to 20-nm-thick NPC mimics.
source: Note that the estimated grafting density is approximately one order of magnitude lower compared to 20-nm-thick NPC mimics (Ananth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and cited from Ananth et al., 2018.

claim: Comparable protein densities of 50–150 mg/mL are still obtained because the relatively long channel of the ZMW pores prevents the Nsp1 molecules from spilling out of the pore.
source: Yet, we still obtain comparable protein densities of 50–150 mg/mL because the relatively long channel of the ZMW pores prevents the Nsp1 molecules from spilling out of the pore as in the case for 20-nm-thick SiNx nanopores.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The calculated BSA translocation rates continuously increased with increasing diameter and reproduced the trend of the experimental data well.
source: The calculated BSA translocation rates continuously increased with increasing diameter and reproduced the trend of the experimental data well (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A delayed onset of the BSA translocation rate for Nsp1-coated pores was observed with an offset of 9.9 ± 0.1 nm, which compares well to the experimental value of 11.5 ± 0.4 nm.
source: Similar to the experimental data, we observed a delayed onset of the BSA translocation rate for Nsp1-coated pores with an offset of 9.9 ± 0.1 nm, which compares quite well to the experimental value of 11.5 ± 0.4 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The computed selectivity ratios for a grafting density of 1 Nsp1 per 300 nm² are in good agreement with the experimental values.
source: The computed selectivity ratios for a grafting density of 1 Nsp1 per 300 nm2 are in good agreement with the experimental values (Figure 5D), especially given that we basically only employ a single fitting parameter.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At pore diameters below 60 nm, the Nsp1 mesh remained closed over the entire duration of the simulation and the highest protein density was found along the central axis.
source: At pore diameters below 60 nm, the Nsp1 mesh remained closed over the entire duration of the simulation and the highest protein density was found along the central axis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: For pore diameters above 60 nm, the highest protein density was found at the pore walls, and the transient formation of a central channel was observed that became persistent at pore diameters above 80 nm.
source: For pore diameters above 60 nm, however, the highest protein density was found at the pore walls (Figure 5E), and we observed the transient formation of a central channel that became persistent at pore diameters above 80 nm (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: Despite the transient appearance of a central channel at pore diameters of 60 nm, the predicted translocation rates increased continuously and followed the quadratic model over the whole range of probed diameters.
source: Despite the transient appearance of a central channel at pore diameters of 60 nm and the shift of the highest protein density away from the center, the predicted translocation rates increased continuously and followed the quadratic model over the whole range of probed diameters (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For diameters below 60 nm, the distribution of the voids was homogeneous across the Nsp1 mesh, suggesting the absence of a preferred pathway.
source: For diameters below 60 nm, the distribution of the voids was homogeneous across the Nsp1 mesh, suggesting the absence of a preferred pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: For diameters above 60 nm, the distribution of voids closely followed the time-averaged protein density inside the pores, confirming that most BSA translocations occur through the central channel of the Nsp1 mesh.
source: For diameters above 60 nm, the distribution of voids closely followed the time-averaged protein density inside the pores, confirming that most BSA translocations occur through the central channel of the Nsp1 mesh.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Small pores below 50 nm showed a moderate increase in selectivity at a Kap95 concentration of 1 µM compared to the absence of Kap95.
source: For small pores (< 50 nm), we observed a moderate increase of the selectivity ratio at 1000 nM Kap95 compared to lower concentrations of Kap95 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: An almost twofold increase of the Kap95 translocation rate for small pores at 1000 nM compared to 100 nM was found, which was absent for large pores.
source: Interestingly, we found an almost twofold increase of the Kap95 translocation rate for small pores at 1000 nM compared to 100 nM, which was absent for large pores (see Appendix 11—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Appendix 11—figure 1.

claim: The reduction of the translocation rate for BSA and the increase for Kap95 resulted in an increase of the apparent selectivity for small pores to 7.1 ±1.6 at a Kap95 concentration of 1000 nM.
source: Combined, the reduction of the translocation rate for BSA and the increase for Kap95 resulted in an increase of the apparent selectivity for small pores to 7.1 ±1.6 at a Kap95 concentration of 1000 nM.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: No effect of the BSA concentration on the translocation rates of Kap95 was observed.

claim: The binding of Kap95 to the FG-Nup mesh increased the selectivity of Nsp1-coated pores, leading to a reduction of the BSA translocation rate.

claim: Larger pores above 60 nm showed a lower selectivity at all Kap95 concentrations compared to small Nsp1 pores.

claim: A considerable reduction to almost the bare pore selectivity was observed for 1000 nM Kap95 in large pores.

claim: The estimated effective layer thickness in the absence of Kap95 is approximately 12 nm, which agrees well with measurements on flat surfaces.

source: While no significant change was detected at 100 nM Kap95, we observed a drastic decrease of the estimated layer thickness by a factor of ≈ 2 at 1000 nM Kap95 compared to the absence of Kap95 (Figure 6G), suggesting that the Nsp1 layer collapsed as it was occupied by Kap95.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The optical approach offers several advantages compared to conductance-based nanopore measurements, including a superior signal-to-noise ratio, excellent specificity for the labeled analyte, increased throughput, no limitations on pore size, and the potential to add unlabeled components.
source: Our approach offers several advantages compared to conductance-based nanopore measurements (Kowalczyk et al., 2011; Ananth et al., 2018; Fragasso et al., 2021; Fragasso et al., 2022), namely a superior signal-to-noise ratio (see Appendix 3), an excellent specificity for the labeled analyte that enables simultaneous detection of different components, increased throughput by measuring multiple pores in a single experiment, no limitations on pore size, and the potential to add unlabeled components while still investigating their effects.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: The approach allows measurement of translocations by free diffusion in the absence of an external electric field.
source: Importantly, our approach also allows us to measure translocations by free diffusion in the absence of an external electric field, which may potentially bias the experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: The 90-nm-long channel used here is approximately three times longer than the native NPC.

claim: Repeated detection of the same molecule leads to an overestimation of the event rate compared to the actual translocation rate by approximately a factor of 2.

claim: Combined, this resulted in an approximately 6 times lower translocation rate compared to what is predicted from Fick's law.
source: Combined, this resulted in an ≈ 6 times lower translocation rate compared to what is predicted from Fick's law, potentially due to the hydrodynamic pressure applied in our experiments (Auger et al., 2014), protein–pore interactions, and missing of low-signal events by the detection algorithm.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and cited from Auger et al., 2014.

claim: Compared to the study of Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009, an order of magnitude higher event rates of approximately 0.04 Hz/nM for pores of similar size were found.
source: Compared to the study of Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009, who report values of 0.003 Hz/nM obtained from bulk studies on 30 nm pores, we find an order of magnitude higher event rates of approximately 0.04 Hz/nM for pores of similar size.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and cited from Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009.

claim: The discrepancy with Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009 can be explained by the fact that the functionalized pores were placed at the ends of 6-μm-long channels, which is expected to considerably reduce the translocation rates.
source: This discrepancy can be explained by the fact that the functionalized pores used by Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009 were placed at the ends of 6-μm-long channels, which is expected to considerably reduce the translocation rates.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and cited from Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009.

source: The absence of a discrete step in the experimental selectivity at a specific pore diameter is thus at odds with a static picture of either an extended or collapsed Nsp1-mesh but rather supports a dynamic transition between both states for intermediate pore diameters.
